html:
The Krahô, who call themselves Mehin, are an Indigenous people of the dry savanna of northern Tocantins, Brazil. They belong to the Timbira group of the Jê-speaking peoples, like the Canela and the Apinajé.

They live in round villages, with houses set in a ring around a central plaza, linked by paths like the spokes of a wheel. Their ceremonies include log races, in which two teams run carrying heavy logs. They farm, hunt and gather.

Cattle ranchers moved into their land in the 1800s. In 1940 ranchers attacked two Krahô villages and killed many people. After this, the government of Brazil set aside the Kraolândia reserve for them in the 1940s, and some 3,000 Krahô live there today. Nearby are the Parkatêjê.
